false_alarms.quote: but not of the abstention-habit or the moderation-habit or the courage-habit.
false_alarms.reason: The author gives examples of habits not commonly named, but does not assert that 'nobody' ever talks of them, so 'nobody' is too absolute.
false_alarms.sentence_text: We talk of the smoking habit and the drinking habit, but nobody talks of the courage habit.

false_alarms.quote: It is an invariable part of our Hindoo life to retire for at least half an hour daily into silence, to relax our muscles, govern our breathing, and meditate on eternal things.
false_alarms.reason: The script omits James's important practical example and recommendation that teachers encourage daily relaxation/meditation and moderation of physical tension in pupils.

flags.quote: when people use the word 'habit,' in the majority of instances it is a bad habit which they have in mind.
flags.reason: The chapter says 'in the majority of instances', not 'always', so 'always' is too strong.
flags.sentence_text: James starts with the word itself: when people say "habit", they always mean a bad one.

flags.quote: but not of the abstention-habit or the moderation-habit or the courage-habit.
flags.reason: The author gives examples of habits not commonly named, but does not assert that 'nobody' ever talks of them, so 'nobody' is too absolute.
flags.sentence_text: We talk of the smoking habit and the drinking habit, but nobody talks of the courage habit.

flags.quote: I believe that we are subject to the law of habit in consequence of the fact that we have bodies.
flags.reason: James attributes habit to bodily/nervous plasticity, not to free will.
flags.sentence_text: James believes it is because we have free will.

flags.quote: just as a sheet of paper or a coat, once creased or folded, tends to fall forever afterward into the same identical folds.
flags.reason: James uses the paper/coat creasing simile, not a river; the river example does not match the text.
flags.sentence_text: He compares this to a river: it never flows over the same ground twice.

flags.quote: Ninety-nine hundredths or, possibly, nine hundred and ninety-nine thousandths of our activity is purely automatic and habitual, from our rising in the morning to our lying down each night.
flags.reason: The chapter claims almost all activity is habitual (very large fraction), not 'about half' as the script states.
flags.sentence_text: James says that about half of what we do, from rising in the morning to lying down at night, is purely automatic and habitual.

flags.quote: I remember long ago reading in an Austrian paper the advertisement of a certain Rudolph Somebody, who promised fifty gulden reward to any one who after that date should find him at the wine-shop of Ambrosius So-and-so.
flags.reason: The chapter says the advertisement was in an Austrian paper, not a German one.
flags.sentence_text: His example is a man called Rudolph, who advertised in a German paper that he would pay fifty gulden to anyone who found him at a certain wine-shop.

flags.quote: Each lapse is like the letting fall of a ball of string which one is carefully winding up: a single slip undoes more than a great many turns will wind again.
flags.reason: The chapter says a single lapse undoes more than many turns will wind again, but the script's wording ('you lose a turn, and you wind it again') reverses the intended meaning.
flags.sentence_text: Each lapse is like dropping a ball of string that you are carefully winding up: you lose a turn, and you wind it again.

flags.quote: It is not in the moment of their forming, but in the moment of their producing motor effects, that resolves and aspirations communicate the new 'set' to the brain.
flags.reason: The chapter insists the brain is set when resolutions produce motor action, not at the moment of forming, so the script's claim of both moments is incorrect.
flags.sentence_text: Resolves give the brain its new set in the moment when they are formed, and again in the moment when they produce action.

flags.quote: The loss of these tastes is a loss of happiness, and may possibly be injurious to the intellect, and more probably to the moral character, by enfeebling the emotional part of our nature.
flags.reason: The chapter hedges that loss 'may possibly' injure the intellect; the script's 'certainly injurious' is too strong.
flags.sentence_text: Darwin thought that the loss of these tastes was a loss of happiness, and that it is certainly injurious to the intellect.

flags.quote: but, if not persistently fed with the appropriate matter, instead of growing into a powerful and necessary habit, it atrophies and dies, choked by the rival interests to which the daily food is given.
flags.reason: The author attributes loss of tastes to neglect and atrophy, not to an inevitable consequence of a scientific life, so the script's general conclusion about scientists is not drawn by James.
flags.sentence_text: James concludes that people who give their lives to science, as Darwin did, cannot keep a taste for poetry.

flags.quote: for sudden conversions, however infrequent they may be, unquestionably do occur.
flags.reason: James explicitly allows that sudden conversions do occur, so saying he answers that they 'never really occur' misstates him.
flags.sentence_text: He answers that sudden conversions never really occur, and so his laws stand: an old habit cannot be broken at one stroke.
